extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, epistemology, and the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and limits for evaluating inductive inferences and generalizations in science and common reasoning; distinguishes types of induction, their trustworthiness, and when methods of testing apply. Discusses causation, uniformities of succession and co-existence, and the epistemic status of kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of the law of causation (assumed by inductive methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of the law of causation is assumed in them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive methods presuppose that every event has some antecedent cause; this assumption underlies Agreement/Difference/Concomitant Variation methods. Mill notes this is often taken for granted and that using it in proofs can be a petitio principii; proponents sometimes appeal to instinct to justify it, but such belief is not itself proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief is not evidence; appeal to senses and consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief is not proof, and does not dispense with the necessity of proof. Evidence is not that which the mind does or must yield to, but that which it ought to yield to; an appeal from the judging faculty to the faculties of sense and consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a proposition merely because it is widely or instinctively believed. Proper evidence must make belief conformable to fact; hence inductive claims should be tested against sensory/conscious experience rather than psychological propensity to believe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction per enumerationem simplicem (simple enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization of an observed fact from the mere absence of any known instance to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This early, 'inartificial' mode of induction is fallible and often precarious, though it can provide sufficient assurance in many ordinary cases (e.g., food nourishes, fire burns). There is a scale of trustworthiness: better for very wide, widely-diffused regularities than for narrow specializations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific induction as improvement by less fallible operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvement consists in correcting one of these inartificial generalizations by means of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific induction substitutes less fallible procedures (e.g., Mill’s Four Methods) to test and strengthen generalizations. A generalization should be tested by showing it follows from, or conflicts with, a stronger induction or broader empirical foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness inversely proportional to particularity of generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The precariousness of the method of simple enumeration is in an inverse ratio to the largeness of the generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple enumeration is more likely to mislead when the subject-matter is special and limited; as the domain of the generalization widens, simple enumeration becomes less liable to error and may suffice for broad truths (e.g., principles of number or geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for affirming an empirical law as effectively universal
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject-matter of any generalization is so widely diffused that there is no time, no place, and no combination of circumstances but must afford an example either of its truth or of its falsity, and if it be never found otherwise than true, its truth cannot be contingent on any collocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirm a generalization as an empirical law (co-extensive with human experience) only when the number and dispersion of confirming cases exceed what can reasonably be ascribed to chance, and when plausible counteracting circumstances could scarcely have escaped notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the law of causation to confer certainty on narrower inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of cause and effect, being thus certain, is capable of imparting its certainty to all other inductive propositions which can be deduced from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor generalizations should be regarded as proved only insofar as they can be connected with or derived from the more universal law of causation. Scientific induction often seeks such embedding to increase confidence in narrower claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claims to the range of observation; do not overextend induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The uniformity in the succession of events ... must be received not as a law of the universe, but of that portion of it only which is within the range of our means of sure observation, with a reasonable degree of extension to adjacent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extending empirical laws beyond the domain where we have reliable observation. Extrapolation to radically different contexts (e.g., distant stellar regions) is speculative and lacks evidential support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existences between effects must depend on their causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Between phenomena which are themselves effects, the co-existences must necessarily depend on the causes of those phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two effects co-exist regularly, this uniformity suggests their causes co-exist or are coordinated. Use causal analysis to explain co-existence (examples: tides, simultaneous eclipses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformities of co-existence among ultimate properties (Kinds) may not be causal
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be one class of co-existences which cannot depend on causation: the co-existences between the ultimate properties of things—those properties which are the causes of all phenomena, but are not themselves caused by any phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements about Kinds (e.g., 'all crows are black') assert co-existences of properties that may be ultimate features of the Kind rather than effects of causes; their justification differs from causal inductive methods and may be more problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ultimate properties from derivative (caused) properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Some properties are ultimate; others are derivative and dependent on causes. Of chemical compounds and organized beings, many specific properties are consequent on their elements or causes; elementary substances more likely possess ultimate properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat generalizations about compounds cautiously—their properties may be explained by underlying causes and so are empirical. Resolution into simpler laws can reclassify properties from 'ultimate' to derivative, altering the status of associated generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of Agreement/Difference (elimination) not generally applicable to co-existences of Kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no room for elimination; no method of Agreement or Difference, or of Concomitant Variations ... We cannot conclude that the blackness we see in crows must be an invariable property of crows merely because there is nothing else present of which it can be an invariable property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The elimination principle (Baconian method) applies to succession/causation but fails for co-existence claims about Kinds because there is no analogue of 'every effect must have a cause.' Avoid applying causal elimination methods to infer properties of kinds without independent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test and improve generalizations by embedding or resolving into broader laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To test a generalization, by showing that it either follows from, or conflicts with, some stronger induction, some generalization resting on a broader foundation of experience, is the beginning and end of the logic of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve the reliability of inductive claims by seeking broader, less fallible inductions that subsume them, or by resolving apparent exceptions into explanations involving counteracting causes; where possible, show how a purported generalization is a consequence of a more secure law.
